>October 21, 2026 Announcing Cohere's Rerank 5 Models We’re pleased to announce the release of Rerank 5 , Cohere’s most advanced reranking models for enterprise retrieval: sharper search, with fewer tokens sent to your LLM. Rerank 5 Pro delivers our highest reranking quality yet, with its largest gains on reasoning-intensive retrieval and in enterprise domains such as finance, healthcare, and scientific research. Context Focus : An optional capability that returns the most relevant passages within each document, as scored character spans, in the same Rerank call. Pass only those passages to your LLM to cut token costs, or highlight them to show users why a result matched. Calibrated relevance scores : Scores are consistent across queries and domains, so you can set one threshold to decide which results reach your LLM. https://deepmind.google/blog/gemini-omni.xd:
Google DeepMind has released Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, a video model that can now create and edit clips up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds in Omni 1.1. Users can set the length in one-second steps from 3 to 15 seconds, which makes it possible to tell a full story, make a product explainer, or produce a complete social ad in one go.

The update also brings better consistency and reference following. Users can guide generation with images of characters, products, or styles, short motion clips of up to three seconds, and audio cues, and the model keeps those details steady from the first frame to the last. Faces, clothing, packaging text, and brand colors stay the same across camera angles, which helps with virtual try-on videos, product spins, and branded ads.

Multi-turn conversational editing is another new feature. Instead of starting over, users can change a clip step by step, for example by swapping a product or background, changing the lighting or weather, or switching the aspect ratio. The same editing works across full 15-second clips, so creating ad versions for different audiences and placements takes less effort.

Dialogue and camera work have also improved. Scenes can include more natural-sounding speech, clearer lip-sync, and separate voices for multiple speakers. The model can also handle complex camera moves, such as fast flythroughs, dramatic zoom-outs, and orbits, with fewer unwanted jump cuts and a steadier, more cinematic look.

The price has dropped 30% compared with Omni 1.1, to $0.07 per second for 720p video. Users can draft quickly at 360p or 720p, fix details with follow-up edits, and then upscale their best versions to 1080p or 4K. This approach is meant to keep costs down.

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is now generally available through the Gemini API and Gemini for business, and it is also rolling out in Google Vids and Flow. Google says businesses, startups, and creators are already using it. The release comes with Google Cloud's enterprise-grade infrastructure and security, and Provisioned Throughput is available. All outputs carry an imperceptible SynthID watermark.

Google notes that it is still working on improving fast sports action, rapid script changes, and complex physics. Even so, the company says the model is well suited to businesses, developers, and creators who need to make videos at scale.

https://deepmind.google/blog/gemini-4-ca.xd:
Google DeepMind has announced Gemini 4 Carbon, its newest and strongest AI model, which it describes as having state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities.

On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, version 5.0, Carbon ranks first with a score of 59. It shows large gains in coding and agentic tasks, as well as in skills needed for cybersecurity. Its scores include 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for finding vulnerabilities, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploitation, and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching. On internal tests, it also produces more secure code and shows lower rates of misalignment and fabrication in live coding environments.

Carbon follows Gemini 4 Argon, which launched two weeks earlier. Google says its researchers and models are working together to move capabilities forward while strengthening safeguards at the same time.

The rollout will be gradual. Starting this week, Carbon will be available to a subset of cyber defenders, and access will expand to more trusted partners through the Fairwind Program. Google is also taking part in the U.S. government's voluntary process for testing models before release. The company is still gathering feedback and refining guardrails before offering Carbon to developers, businesses, and consumers as soon as possible.

Carbon is designed for much harder, long-running engineering work. Google says its teams have seen it run for days, working through dead ends to solve complex, multi-step problems such as finding and fixing subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems.

Based on user feedback, Google improved performance in coding, agentic and scientific tasks, full-stack web development, and multimodal understanding. Better output quality in web development moved Carbon up 89 Elo points to rank fourth on WebDev Arena, with a score of 1768.

In cybersecurity, Carbon achieves top performance across vulnerability detection, validation, and remediation. On internal benchmarks, its success rate for generating secure code is more than double that of Argon. The Chrome team reported that Carbon performed more than 10 times better than another lab's large frontier model at generating high-quality patches. Wiz, a cloud security platform, also found Carbon leading on web penetration testing benchmarks, a core capability for its Scan for Good initiative.

Google says Carbon performs strongly on key external benchmarks, evaluated without guardrails. Its safety approach builds on Argon's multi-layered stack, which combines model training, real-time misuse defenses, resistance to prompt injection, and chain-of-thought monitoring. Google says it went further on alignment with Carbon, training the model to respond appropriately to complex or high-pressure tasks.

Carbon will launch at the same introductory price as Argon: $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens priced 95% below the input rate. After the introductory period ends, the price will rise to $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens.

https://deepmind.google/blog/genie-4-a-n.xd:
Google DeepMind has announced Genie 4, a new world model that it says produces more realistic, real-time interactive simulations. Genie 4 can generate sound along with the visuals, including music, ambient noise, and spoken dialogue, all at the same time as the world itself.

The model builds on capabilities from the Gemini family. Gemini Omni helps anchor the simulations in real-world appearance and behavior, while other Gemini models handle the reasoning needed to keep a simulation coherent and continuous over time.

Users can start an event and Genie 4 simulates what follows, including how the environment responds, how it sounds, and how the people in it move, react, and speak. Google says understanding and simulating the world is a crucial part of building artificial general intelligence. It presents Genie 4 as a way to create safe, highly varied simulations for training robots and AI agents, and for making new interactive experiences.

Genie 4 is being released first as a research preview to trusted testers. Google plans to gather feedback before a wider release to consumers and developers. The first group to get access will be Google AI Ultra subscribers using Project Genie, along with early access partners of the Gemini API and Google AI Studio. People can join the waitlist for Genie 4 in Project Genie through a link on the announcement page.

According to the announcement, Genie 4 improves photorealism, movement, and native audio. The sounds in the examples were produced directly by the model. The examples include recordings of real-time sessions in which users navigate with standard keyboard controls, move the camera, and type text prompts to steer the scene as it changes.

Users can change a running simulation with natural language, for example by changing the weather, moving the camera, or adding a new person or object. Gemini adapts each prompt to fit the existing scene and keeps the world developing consistently between user inputs.

Genie 4 is also described as having a better physical understanding of the world. It simulates physics such as aerodynamics and collisions. Google says its largest improvement is in how it simulates people, who move naturally, respond to their surroundings, and can be steered in real time.

The announcement describes Genie 4 as the first real-time world model to generate audio natively. Each world carries the ambient sound of its setting, such as wind in trees or waves at a beach. Google says the bigger challenge is human speech, and states that Genie 4 supports interactive dialogue in which characters talk and react to user input or events in real time.

Google also says Genie 4 works with Gemini to add a layer of reasoning. In this setup, Gemini 3.8 Flash acts as a guiding agent. It watches the scene as it is generated, breaks a goal into steps, checks incoming frames to confirm each step succeeded, and changes its plan when the world shifts or a user steps in. Google says this allows worlds with reliable cause and effect and multi-step reasoning, which can be used to test how AI systems handle different environments before they are used in the real world.

The announcement also covers experiments that combine Genie 4 with an experimental model called Gemini 4 Argon and with Gemini Robotics. In one example, Argon splits a user's instruction into steps, and Genie 4 renders them while the simulation runs. The example shows a humanoid robot from Apptronik named Apollo playing checkers. Google says that because Genie 4 can be steered with text during a simulation, the simulation can adapt as the task progresses.

Google describes Genie 4 as an early and experimental model. It has been tested with groups of trusted testers in creative industries, journalism, education, gaming, and engineering. Testers said the improvements in photorealism, native audio, and real-time steering help them turn ideas into realistic simulations.

Google also points to hybrid world models as a promising direction. These would combine the structured reasoning of language models with pixel-level simulation. Gemini would plan the story and structure, while Genie would generate how the world looks, sounds, and responds.

On safety, Google says Genie 4 has strict guardrails that match its policies for other models, and that it ran internal safety evaluations before the preview to prevent harmful or malicious content. All video and audio generated by Genie 4 will include SynthID, Google's imperceptible watermark for identifying AI-generated content.

Google notes several limits. Over short sessions Genie 4 can keep environments coherent, but visual details and object permanence can drift over longer runs, after many edits, or while moving through a scene. Complex physical interactions, real-time audio accuracy, legible text, spatial accuracy, and long-term consistency are still being researched. Genie 4 will be available to Google AI Ultra subscribers in Project Genie and to early access partners in the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, and the waitlist is open now.

https://mistral.ai/news/voxtral-3/.xd:
Voxtral 3 is a new set of speech tools from Mistral, announced as a voice agent SDK plus speech models for real-time, multi-step conversations in more than 50 languages. The system combines accurate transcription, natural speech with emotional adaptability, and deep tool integration. It is available through Mistral's EU-hosted API or for self-deployment, which lets organizations keep their data under their own control. Mistral says it is aimed at contact centers, virtual assistants, and hands-free copilots.

Mistral explains that speech transcription and voice generation have improved, but building voice agents that can listen, reason, speak, and carry out complex tasks is still hard. A reliable agent must listen accurately across languages, accents, speakers, and interruptions. It must also reason about what users mean, speak naturally with emotion, and take action across several connected systems. Doing all of this reliably in real time is the challenge Voxtral 3 is meant to address.

Voxtral 3 is a family of speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, along with a voice agent SDK. The SDK puts listening, thinking, tool calling, and speaking into one real-time streaming pipeline. Mistral says the goal is natural conversations, with agents that can understand nuanced requests and carry out multi-step actions across connected systems.

The speech-to-text model, Voxtral Small Transcribe 3, supports transcription in more than 50 languages. It can identify who is speaking, use key phrases to improve accuracy, and detect when someone has finished talking so agents can respond without delay. The text-to-speech model, Voxtral Mini TTS 3, offers new voices that change emotion, pace, and emphasis based on context. It supports more than 35 languages and more than 50 dialects.

Mistral also offers Pro Voice, which adapts a voice more closely than basic cloning. It can reproduce a speaker's distinctive character, emotional range, and speaking style across languages, using about 30 minutes of audio. The company says the whole family is built for sovereign deployment, so organizations can decide where audio is processed, how data is handled, and whether conversations are kept. Voxtral 3 can be used through Mistral's EU-hosted API or on the customer's own infrastructure.

Mistral reports that Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 leads on diarization and multilingual transcription, including in English, French, and Spanish, and says it outperforms Whisper, Scribe v2, and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe. Its smaller Mini variant has 4 billion parameters and costs $0.0035 per minute. Both transcription models support context biasing, where key terms can be supplied to improve recognition of technical words without fine-tuning. The company's benchmark charts compare word error rates and keyphrase recall, with lower error rates and higher recall being better.

Voxtral Realtime Transcribe 3 is built for agent use and provides transcription with latency under 500 milliseconds in more than 35 languages. It also supports diarization and context biasing. Mistral says its text-to-speech model, Voxtral Mini TTS 3, is available in batch and realtime modes, supports more than 35 languages and 50 dialects, and costs $13 per million characters. The company says this is less than comparable models from OpenAI, Deepgram, ElevenLabs, and Gemini. Newer features include voice cloning from more than 30 minutes of audio, custom instruction following, contextual speech, and a vocabulary library, with controls for emotion, pacing, and emphasis.

Mistral has also published evaluation results for speech quality. These cover pronunciation of rare and made-up words, performance across 11 languages, and expressive English speech, with scores from an automated judge. The charts show Voxtral generally scoring well against other systems, though the company's own tests are internal.

The voice agent SDK, built on LiveKit, runs speech input, reasoning, and speech output as one streaming pipeline. Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime 3 detects when a caller has finished, a general model such as Mistral Small 4 handles reasoning and tool calls, and Voxtral TTS replies in the tone of the conversation. Mistral says each turn completes in under one second, and the agent stops speaking when the caller interrupts. During calls, the agent can verify identity, check a bill, or book an appointment, using function calling, web search, and retrieval from the customer's own systems. It can handle phone calls over SIP and browser or app calls over WebRTC, and it connects to existing telephony and contact-center software. Each stage is a separate model, so the language model, voice, or language can be changed without rewriting the agent.

Voxtral 3 is available now through the Mistral API, with European, US, and global endpoints. Users can try voice agents, transcription, speech generation, and voice cloning in the Studio playgrounds. Organizations that want to run the full stack on their own premises or in a private cloud can contact Mistral's team. The three main models are listed as Voxtral Small Transcribe 3 for flagship transcription and diarization, Voxtral Transcribe 3 for low-latency transcription and diarization, Voxtral Realtime Transcribe 3 for configurable realtime agent use, and Voxtral TTS for speech with zero-shot and professional voice cloning, 35+ languages, 50+ dialects, and streaming.

https://mistral.ai/news/timestral/.xd:
Mistral has released Timestral, its first family of time-series foundation models, which are used to make forecasts from data collected over time. The models make probabilistic, multivariate forecasts and can use past-only and known-future covariates. Timestral is available in four sizes, from 5M to 209M parameters.

The largest model, at 209M parameters, ranks first on all three of the field's main public benchmarks: GIFT-Eval, TIME, and fev-bench. It outperforms the previous state of the art while using only two-thirds of the parameters. Results have been submitted to the GIFT-Eval and TIME leaderboards.

Across the three benchmarks, Timestral ranks first among pre-trained, zero-shot models on all five metrics. These results come from a single checkpoint, without ensembling.

The four models are 5M, 28M, 123M and 209M parameters. The larger models forecast better, while the smaller ones are faster and cheaper. All four share the same architecture and training recipe, and each size sits on the Pareto front of accuracy versus model size, meaning no public model forecasts better at that size.

The 28M model beats Chronos-2, which is about four times larger, on GIFT-Eval and TIME. The 209M model beats TimesFM-3 and Falcon-2.0 while using fewer parameters.

Timestral does not need a GPU to run. On a standard server CPU with 8 threads, forecasting one day ahead from three weeks of 15-minute history takes 17 ms with the 5M model and 113 ms with the 209M model. The 28M model is 3.6 times faster than the 209M model, and the 123M model comes within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency.

To illustrate its uses, the article describes an industrial plant with thousands of sensors. Timestral can model related sensors together, so it uses the links between them instead of forecasting each one alone. It predicts a full range of likely values, so teams can see the uncertainty and plan around risk. It can also take categorical inputs, such as a machine's state, without turning them into numbers, and it can use known future factors, such as production schedules or weather forecasts.

Timestral can run inside existing monitoring systems or work with Mistral's language models in multi-step agent workflows. In the plant example, Timestral watches sensor streams and flags anomalies. An agent then compares the flagged signals with past failures, starts sub-agents to investigate causes using maintenance records, logs, manuals and other data, and drafts a suggested diagnosis with evidence and next steps for the plant manager.

The results come from several techniques. Decoupled Horizon Forecasting keeps the full history as context while the model predicts the future. Covariate-aware attention assigns each input a role so that known future information can be used without leaking a target's future. Most of the training data is synthetic, generated to have trends, seasonality and nonlinear links between series. Training happens in two stages: first on purely synthetic data with a context size of 8192, then on a mix of real and synthetic data with a context four times longer. The objective is a pinball loss over 21 quantiles, a discrete approximation of CRPS. More detail is in the technical report.

Public benchmarks may not match production data, which can differ in behavior and structure and can shift over time. For this reason, organisations can adapt Timestral through Mistral Forge, the same training pipeline Mistral uses for its language models. Forge supports architectural extensions such as domain-specific covariates, fine-tuning on proprietary data while keeping general performance, and control over the training data, including adjusting the mix, replaying pre-training data, and generating synthetic samples for the target domain. The full pipeline can be deployed on clients' hardware, including air-gapped environments.

A GitHub repository is available for running Timestral on your own data. For more specialised forecasting problems or research collaboration, readers are invited to contact Mistral.

https://x.ai/news/grok-voice-3.xd:
SpaceXSI (formerly xAI), the maker of Grok, has announced Grok Voice 3.0, which it describes as its most capable speech-to-speech model.

The company says the model sets a new record for resolving customer support calls, responds in under one second, and costs less to run than other leading models.

Grok Voice currently handles millions of conversations each day across Tesla and SpaceX products. Grok Voice 3.0 is available today through the API, priced the same as its predecessor, Grok Voice 2.0.

Artificial Analysis, an independent tester, ranks Grok Voice 3.0 first on its Speech-to-Speech Index with a score of 86.9. That index combines speech reasoning, τ-Voice, and results from blind head-to-head calls measuring preference and task success.

The model also scores 97% on Full Duplex Bench, which measures how naturally it handles pauses, taking turns in conversation, and interruptions.

On τ-Voice, which tests how well agents handle support calls with varied accents, background noise, and interruptions, Grok Voice 3.0 scores 71.6%. That is close to GPT-Live-1 (Astra), but the company says its response time is 40% lower.

Cost is another point of comparison. In Artificial Analysis's Big Bench Audio run, which measures what each model costs to complete a task, Grok Voice 3.0 came in below both GPT-Live-1 (Astra, Medium) and GPT-Realtime-2.1.

On EVA-Bench, a benchmark from ServiceNow for enterprise voice agents, Grok Voice 3.0 achieved the highest accuracy score, at 74%. It also performed best when accuracy and customer experience were scored together.

In Tesla vehicles, the model supports drivers with simple requests such as checking a calendar or answering an email, as well as larger tasks like ordering coffee or booking dinner, all hands-free. It also powers the voice mode of Grok Bot.

Starlink call centers use Grok Voice to answer 20,000 customer calls each day in several languages. About 70% are resolved without a human agent, and one in four sales calls ends in a purchase before the caller hangs up. A single agent built on the model can verify customers, troubleshoot hardware, issue credits, and ship replacement equipment.

Grok Voice 3.0 is available today in the Speech to Speech API at $0.08 per minute, or $4.80 per hour, the same rate as Grok Voice 2.0. Agents using grok-voice-latest were switched over automatically and need no changes.

https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt.xd:
OpenAI has introduced GPT-6 Cyber, a cybersecurity model that is better at finding and fixing software weaknesses and more reliable about staying within the limits that researchers set. It shows major gains over GPT-5.6 Cyber on key tests, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym, and a large step forward on staying within scope.

On ExploitGym, which measures whether a model can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT-6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber. In a separate alignment test, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and in 100% of tests with that prompt. OpenAI says this came from dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.

The model is already being used on real software. OpenAI researchers used it to develop 948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux and to identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, even though those systems had already been tested extensively with frontier models. It also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has released fixes for many of the Firefox issues. Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and OpenAI has used it to find and fix weaknesses in its own infrastructure.

OpenAI says there is a limited window to use advanced models to secure software, and it plans to expand its Daybreak program to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers. Security researchers at Apiiro found that Claude Code, an AI coding tool, is accidentally exposing sensitive information in public GitHub repositories. They found thousands of secrets, including database passwords, API tokens, and root logins, inside Claude Code settings files stored in those repositories.

The problem comes from how Claude Code handles approval for automated shell commands. When a user selects "Yes, and don't ask again" to approve a command, that choice is saved as a rule in a local settings file called ".claude/settings.local.json." The command is often saved exactly as written, including any sensitive information it contains.

On a user's own computer, this is generally not a serious issue. Anthropic's documentation says the settings file is added to the developer's global .gitignore list, which usually keeps it from being shared publicly. However, that protection does not carry over to the repository level. If a repository is cloned to another machine, or if a folder later becomes a repository, the file can be uploaded by accident. Apiiro says Claude Code itself will often commit changes to the file without the user's input.

Apiiro's researchers found more than 100,000 cases where the settings file had been uploaded to a public GitHub repository. About 1,100 of these, from 63 different organizations, contained secrets such as public API tokens, database passwords, or private keys. Even after a file is removed from a repository, the secrets can remain in forks of the project if users are not careful.

The issue was first flagged in a Claude Code bug report in August 2025. Other reports noted that the settings file was sometimes not added to .gitignore, or that sensitive commands could be saved to a file without git protection. These reports were closed without action after 60 days of inactivity.

Boris Cherny of the Claude Code team said on Hacker News over the weekend that the team is "looking into what we can do to prevent this." He said these files should almost never be checked into a user's git source control and that such cases seemed to happen only when the files were manually created and checked in. He recommended Claude Code's auto mode, which uses classifiers to handle routine permission prompts without manual allow and deny lists. When another user pointed out that sensitive commands can still be saved to settings files in auto mode, Cherny said the team is working on improving this.

Cherny also recommended that users run secret scanners, tools that search files for sensitive information and remove it. He said the team is considering building similar scanning into Claude Code in the future. However, Apiiro found that 215 of the roughly 1,100 public secrets in these settings files were missed by two popular scanners, gitleaks and TruffleHog.

This is not the only case of an AI agent accidentally leaking sensitive information. Last month, Meta suspended the sharing feature on its Muse agent after security researchers found that its share links could be easily guessed.

A Google researcher, Pietro Miotti, recently said that a team of AI agents had found a possibly unmapped Maya site in Mexico. The site had already been discovered and published in an academic journal a year earlier. The episode drew criticism from archaeologists online and points to a growing tension in science as amateurs use increasingly powerful AI tools in fields where they lack specialist training.

Miotti said the idea came to him while traveling in Peru, when he wondered what historic explorers might do with modern technology. He chose lidar, a laser-based mapping method that produces detailed three-dimensional images of the land. He set 48 AI agents to search NASA lidar data for signs of undocumented sites. Because public lidar data did not cover Peru well, he focused on the Maya region.

The agents flagged several promising locations, including one major village that did not appear to be in existing records. Miotti described the work to The Verge as a personal side project, done without any Google computing resources or funding. He then contacted Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) to ask whether the site was already known, including through unpublished research. He used the agents to translate his messages into Spanish. INAH told him it had no record of a registered site at that location.

Miotti wrote on his blog that it took less than 72 hours to get from an idea to an official reply from the Mexican government. He called it "by far the best time ever to be alive." He stressed that he is not an archaeologist and said the find would need to be checked through fieldwork. He also said it showed that science was on the brink of a revolution and called for the entire planet to be mapped with lidar. Had he been familiar with the region, he might have noticed that the site was already known and had been documented in an academic journal more than a year before.

Archaeologists quickly pointed out the error on social media. Sarah Parcak, an archaeology professor at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, stressed the importance of checking findings against existing research. She said that a site missing from a government database is not necessarily unknown or unmapped. Other archaeologists criticized the project for spreading misinformation and taking credit away from experts who have used advanced digital tools for decades.

Miotti told The Verge he had not expected so much attention. He said that as a non-archaeologist he had not understood that a site being unregistered is not the same as it being unmapped, and that expert knowledge is needed to verify what the agents find. He acknowledged that his agents and he missed the site. He explained that archaeologists do not usually publish site coordinates, so checking whether a site is known means comparing images with figures in papers, which is much harder for AI agents. He said he updated his blog and post to credit the people who pointed out the error. He still believes agents can help experts sort through large amounts of data, and said archaeologists and PhD students had contacted him interested in the workflow.

Elizabeth Graham, a professor of Mesoamerican archaeology at University College London, told The Verge that the field's problem is not finding new sites. She said many sites in the Maya area are known but have not been explored, excavated, or mapped, and most were found on foot. She also objected to the word "discover," noting that local communities are often already aware of sites in their area. She credited Miotti with doing a decent job using AI to map mounds from lidar data, but said the bigger obstacle is funding. There is not enough money to excavate or map sites as in the past, so finding more sites does not change much.

The episode reflects a wider problem with AI in science. AI tools can produce impressive results, but they often do not engage with the research those results build on. This can lead to claimed breakthroughs that someone else has already made, or to a failure to credit earlier work. Even genuinely new findings can lack the context a specialist would provide, so the job of establishing what was found and why it matters often falls on experts.

Ivan Šprajc, an archaeology professor at the Research Centre of the Slovenian Academy of Sciences and Arts in Ljubljana and a coauthor of the paper documenting the site, told The Verge he was not impressed by the agents' work. He said archaeologists have used lidar and other remote sensing tools for some time, and that spotting something adds little to knowledge on its own. He said contacting INAH was commendable but not enough, because the institution does not have access to all information. The fact that INAH has no record of a site does not mean archaeologists have not seen or explored it.

Šprajc said he worries that AI-assisted amateurs could flood archaeologists with claimed discoveries, noting he had received another such email that day. He also raised the risk that publicizing site locations could attract looters. He said that as long as the findings do not lead to looting, he does not see a major problem.
